title: VPC Networking & Inference Runtime Deep Dive for Private Deployment
summary: Deep dive on networking and runtime perf tradeoffs for a private VPC deployment. Discussed PrivateLink vs peering, NAT egress patterns, DNS resolution (Route53/resolver), ENI limits, and inference runtime concerns (KV cache warm vs cold, batching, quantization). Agreed next steps: Redwood to send network diagram, perf runbook, and pilot checklist; customer to share expected QPS and sample prompts.
topics: Inference runtime: KV cache, batching, quantization, latency vs throughput

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-10 15:30 PDT | Duration approx 55m | Attendees: Aaron Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jonas Meyer (Redwood SRE), Maya Lin (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (Sapphire Health), Tom Alvarez (Sapphire Network), Nadia Ibrahim (Sapphire Security), Ben Foster (Sapphire ML)

00:00 - Aaron Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda: private VPC topology, connectivity options, and then runtime perf questions — batching, KV cache, quantization.
00:18 - Laura Chen: Thanks Aaron. We're looking to run Redwood in our VPC behind strict controls; mainly concerned about egress and keeping traffic inside our accounts as much as possible. Also need guidance on IP usage and DNS.
00:34 - Priya Rao: Great, that's what we'll focus on. One thing upfront — we usually recommend either PrivateLink endpoints or VPC peering depending on your constraints. PrivateLink gives you private ENIs and simplifies DNS but has IP scaling implications.
01:05 - Tom Alvarez: Can you expand on the IP scaling? Our subnets are fairly constrained; we don't want a bunch of ENIs eating up /24s.
01:20 - Jonas Meyer: Sure — with PrivateLink we create an interface endpoint in your subnet. Each endpoint uses an ENI per AZ and depending on concurrency you might need multiple endpoints for throughput; that uses IPs. For heavy throughput we recommend using a dedicated subnet with a larger CIDR or using centralized egress patterns.
01:48 - Tom Alvarez: Hmm, ok. What about peering? We run across accounts so peering might be simpler.
01:55 - Maya Lin: VPC peering works but it exposes routing between VPCs and you need careful route table management; PrivateLink is explicit and doesn't require route propagation. Also with peering you might hit cross-account route limits and you still need NAT for egress if the service requires outbound internet.
02:20 - Nadia Ibrahim: Security question — can we lock down endpoints to specific security groups and only allow TLS? We need SSO and auditability, plus KMS-managed keys for any logs.
02:35 - Aaron Patel: Yes — security groups on interface endpoints, client certs if desired, and we support KMS for at-rest keys. We'll share the security template.
02:50 - Ben Foster: On the runtime side, our biggest concern is latency for streaming responses. We do lots of interactive chat, so 50–200ms p50 token latency matters. How do KV cache and batching affect that?
03:12 - Priya Rao: Good question. Two things: KV cache is the key-value KV cache for autoregressive decoding — it avoids recomputing transformer keys/values for prefixes. Warm cache reduces per-token latency a lot for repeated contexts; cold cache or cache miss will add a few ms to tens of ms depending on model and hardware. Batching increases throughput but will add queuing latency; we use continuous batching and have latency SLO knobs to trade throughput vs p95.
03:42 - Ben Foster: Do you shard KV cache across GPUs or host it externally? We're worried about cross-host network hops.
03:50 - Jonas Meyer: By default cache is co-located on the serving hosts — that gives the lowest latency. For very large contexts or multi-tenant setups we can place a sharded cache in-memory across nodes; cross-host retrievals add network overhead. We also support prefix caching at the edge to reduce cross-host lookups.
04:12 - Laura Chen: So for our private deployment, you recommend co-located KV on the same nodes?
04:20 - Priya Rao: Yes for low latency. If you plan to scale horizontally and expect hot-shard patterns, we'll size the nodes so KV stays local for common prefixes. Also we discussed eviction: LRU with a warm-up phase; you might want to pre-warm with representative prompt sets.
04:42 - Tom Alvarez: Back to networking — egress. If we use PrivateLink, how does outbound egress happen? We want egress through our NATs so we can inspect traffic.
04:55 - Aaron Patel: You can route egress from service instances to your NAT via the configured route tables. If you want all outbound traffic to traverse your inspection stack, put service endpoints in private subnets that route default traffic to your NAT gateway or a proxy. For hosted control-plane callbacks we can also use a private resolver endpoint so DNS resolution stays inside your VPC.
05:20 - Tom Alvarez: What about split-horizon DNS for PrivateLink? We use Route53 private hosted zones for internal names.
05:28 - Maya Lin: We'll provide a DNS pattern: when the endpoint is created, we set up a private DNS name in your zone (via VPC endpoint private DNS). If you have split-horizon, you might need Route53 resolver inbound endpoints or conditional forwarding to ensure the name resolves to the interface IPs in your VPC.
05:50 - Nadia Ibrahim: Any TLS session or keepalive issues with streaming that might be impacted by NAT timeouts?
05:58 - Jonas Meyer: Yes — long-lived streaming can run into NAT idle timeouts. Keep TCP/TLS keepalive alive or use application-level heartbeats. We'll document recommended timeouts. Also keep MTU considerations in mind for large payloads; fragmentation can add CPU overhead.
06:22 - Ben Foster: On quantization — can we go 4-bit without quality regressions? We run clinical summarization and hallucination is a concern.
06:35 - Priya Rao: Quantization provides big cost and throughput wins, but for sensitive tasks we recommend testing with your eval suite. For many models, 4-bit (int4) works fine for generation but you might see small shifts. We can do per-route model selection: higher precision for clinical endpoints, quantized for batch jobs.
06:58 - Laura Chen: How do we validate output quality regressions?
07:04 - Maya Lin: Redwood Optimize offers eval hooks; you can attach prompt sets and automatic regression alerts. For the pilot we'll run a comparative eval on your prompts between full precision and quantized variants.
07:22 - Tom Alvarez: If the service is in our VPC, how do we handle capacity failover? If an AZ goes down, how are ENIs rebalanced?
07:35 - Jonas Meyer: We use multi-AZ deployments. If one AZ loses an endpoint, interface endpoints in other AZs handle traffic if your client is region-aware. There's an ephemeral IP reprovisioning time; we recommend healthchecks and multi-AZ DNS resolution. Also consider using multiple endpoints across AZs in the same subnet or dedicated subnets per AZ.
08:02 - Ben Foster: Are there rate limits per ENI or per endpoint? We're planning bursts of thousands QPS during send times.
08:12 - Aaron Patel: Rate limits are at the service and model level, and we document per-tenant throughput. ENI itself has scaling limits based on instance type and subnet IPs. For bursts, we recommend reserved capacity (Redwood Dedicated) or pre-warmed endpoints and capacity commitments. We'll run a capacity planning exercise for your QPS pattern.
08:40 - Laura Chen: Can you walk through a sample packet flow for a single inference request in our VPC with PrivateLink?
08:47 - Priya Rao: Sure — client in your private subnet -> service ELB or client-side SDK resolves private DNS name to endpoint ENI IP -> TCP TLS to endpoint -> endpoint forwards to Redwood node (stays within backbone) -> model runtime checks KV cache locally -> if cache miss maybe fetch prefix from local neighbor -> generates tokens, streams back over same TLS stream. If the runtime needs to call control plane (logging, callbacks), that can be routed through your NAT or a VPC peered control plane depending on how we set it up.
09:30 - Tom Alvarez: Does the streaming use chunked HTTP/2 or websockets? We prefer HTTP/2 for mTLS.
09:36 - Maya Lin: We support server-sent events and HTTP/2 streaming; mTLS can be supported on private endpoints. We'll map to your preference in the pilot.
09:50 - Ben Foster: For batching, if we have 100 concurrent small requests, does Redwood batch them on the GPU and increase latency? How do you respect latency SLOs?
10:02 - Priya Rao: We do continuous batching with max-latency knobs. You configure target p50/p95; the runtime will flush batches based on time or size. For interactive endpoints you set tight latency windows; for throughput jobs you increase batch windows. We can also set separate routes so chat endpoints use minimal batching and batch export endpoints use aggressive batching.
10:28 - Aaron Patel: And for the KV cache sizing, what inputs do you need from us?
10:34 - Ben Foster: QPS patterns, distribution of prompt lengths, percent of repeated prefixes, and target retention window for cache.
10:42 - Priya Rao: Perfect. Send those and we'll produce a recommended node size and pre-warm strategy.
10:50 - Laura Chen: Any unexpected networking pitfalls customers hit during private deployments?
10:57 - Jonas Meyer: A few: 1) IP exhaustion from lots of interface endpoints in small subnets; 2) NAT idle timeouts breaking long streams; 3) DNS not forwarding to resolver endpoints leading to failed resolution of private names; 4) security group rules inadvertently blocking ephemeral ports for streaming.
11:22 - Tom Alvarez: Regarding route tables, is it better to centralize endpoints in a centralized services VPC and use peering/Transit Gateway?
11:31 - Maya Lin: Centralization reduces IP footprint in app VPCs but adds an extra network hop. Transit Gateway is common for large orgs; still consider the performance hit of routing through TGW and ensure low-latency connectivity. For the lowest latency, colocate endpoints in the same VPC and subnets as clients.
11:54 - Nadia Ibrahim: Audit logs — can we ship them to our Kinesis or S3 with encryption? Also need SOC2 artifacts.
12:03 - Aaron Patel: Yes — we can push logs to your S3 over PrivateLink and support SSE-KMS. We'll attach SOC2 documentation to the follow-up.
12:15 - Ben Foster: One more runtime nit — cache warm-up. How long to pre-warm and what's the effect on p95?
12:25 - Priya Rao: Depends on prompt diversity. With a focused prompt set, pre-warm can be a few minutes to tens of minutes. Warm cache reduces p95 by 30–60% for token generation in some scenarios. We'll quantify in the perf runbook.
12:45 - Laura Chen: Ok, let's recap next steps...
12:52 - Aaron Patel: Recap: Redwood sends network and security templates, KV cache sizing and perf runbook, customer shares QPS and prompts, schedule pilot. Anything else?
13:05 - Nadia Ibrahim: Please include a checklist for compliance review items.
13:10 - Aaron Patel: Will do. Thanks everyone.
13:15 - Meeting end.
